content: The pound-force, often abbreviated as lb, lbf, or simply pound, is a unit of force. It is approximately equivalent to the gravitational force exerted on a mass of one avoirdupois pound at the Earth's surface. Historically, since the 18th century, this unit has been used in low-precision measurements where minor variations in Earth's gravity (which can differ by up to 0.5% depending on location) could be disregarded without significant impact. However, in the 20th century, the need for a more precise definition arose, necessitating the establishment of a standardized value for gravitational acceleration, which was set at 9.80665 m/s². From this standard gravitational acceleration and the international definition of the avoirdupois pound as a unit of mass, the pound-force is defined. Specifically, one avoirdupois pound of mass is equivalent to 16 avoirdupois ounces of mass. Similarly, one ounce-force is defined as one-sixteenth of a pound-force. In certain contexts, such as structural engineering, the term pound is almost exclusively used to denote the unit of force rather than the unit of mass. In other contexts, however, pound may refer to a unit of mass. To avoid ambiguity, the symbols lbf (pounds-force) and lbm (pounds-mass) are often used, along with the explicit terms pounds-force and pounds-mass. There are three common and equally valid foot-pound-second (fps) systems of units used for calculations involving mass and force. These systems are summarized alongside their corresponding metric units. In the engineering fps system, the weight of the mass unit (pound-mass) at Earth's surface is approximately equal to the force unit (pound-force). The proportionality constant in this system is 32.17405 lb·ft/(lbf·s²). The gravitational fps system is a coherent system of units that uses the slug as the unit of mass, thereby eliminating the need for a proportionality constant. Similarly, the absolute fps system is also coherent, and its structure aligns with the SI units used in the absolute metric system.
